日本箏可見於日本宮廷音樂「雅樂」中的樂種，也用於獨奏曲「箏曲」；十七弦箏在合奏中: The koto appears in the genres of Japanese court music, gagaku, and is also used for the solo repertory, sōkyoku; the seventeen-string koto often takes the bass part in ensembles. From the Meiji period onwards the composer Michio Miyagi combined Western music with the traditional koto repertory, and his work for koto and shakuhachi (the end-blown bamboo flute), 'Haru no Umi', has been arranged for many instruments and is also played at New Year in Japan. Kazue Sawai, for her part, arranged John Cage's prepared-piano duet 'Three Dances' for an ensemble of four prepared bass kotos.
日本箏源自中國古箏，七至八世紀傳入日本，初為五弦，後增至七弦。現代形制出於雅樂所: The koto derives from the Chinese guzheng and reached Japan in the seventh or eighth century, at first with five strings and later with seven. The modern form comes from the instrument used in gagaku, which then developed into a solo instrument. Yatsuhashi Kengyō widened the repertory and the tunings and is called the father of the modern koto; after the Meiji restoration, when Western music arrived, Michio Miyagi fused Western and traditional practice, created the seventeen-string bass koto and wrote 'Haru no Umi'. Keiko Nosaka later increased the number of strings to more than twenty.
日本箏為彈撥半管齊特，H-S編號312.22-6，是日本國樂器。琴身多以桐木製成: The koto is a plucked half-tube zither, Hornbostel–Sachs number 312.22-6, and is a national instrument of Japan. The body is usually of paulownia wood and about 180 cm long; it commonly has thirteen strings, tuned on movable bridges, while the seventeen-string version is mostly used for the bass in ensembles. The player plucks with three plectra on the first three fingers of the right hand. The modern form comes from the instrument used in Japanese court music (gagaku) and is found afterwards in both solo and ensemble playing.
日本箏為撥奏半管齊特，弦鳴發聲；常見十三弦，弦下設可移動琴柱調音，不同曲目可用不: The koto is a plucked half-tube zither and sounds by way of its strings; it commonly has thirteen strings, tuned with movable bridges beneath them, and different pieces use different tunings. The player plucks with plectra on three fingers of the right hand. The seventeen-string version takes the bass in ensembles. It belongs with the Chinese guzheng, the Korean gayageum and the Vietnamese đàn tranh in the Asian zither family, but the koto has movable bridges, and there are also bridgeless zither forms. 演奏時將日本箏置於地面，依曲目調整可移動琴橋以定音。發聲以右手前三指佩戴指撥片撥: To play, set the koto on the floor and adjust the movable bridges for the tuning the piece needs. Sound it by plucking with plectra worn on the first three fingers of the right hand; the bridges can also be moved to change the pitch. For a beginner, first check that the bridges are stable, and avoid pressing the strings so hard that a bridge slides or breaks.
琴身與發聲面板傳統以泡桐木製成，木料經乾燥後裁切；表面可鑲嵌象牙、黑檀、玳瑁或金: The body and soundboard are traditionally of paulownia wood, cut after the timber has been dried; the surface may be inlaid with ivory, ebony, tortoiseshell or metal fittings. The bridges were once of ivory, are now mostly plastic and are occasionally wooden.
